newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST-Home shopping woes to depress GUS.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Home shopping woes to depress GUS.

text.p: British catalogues-to-Burberrys group Great Universal Stores Plc is set to report its first annual profit fall in nearly half a century when it publishes results next Thursday.
The market leader in mail order in Britain warned in December difficult trading in its core home shopping business, plus adverse exchange rates would have a significant effect on 1996/97 profits.
Retail analysts predicted pre-tax profits, stripping out tax rebates, would drop to between 547 million and 555 million stg, from 562.3 million in the previous year.
They forecast a dividend of around 18 pence, up from 16.5 million.

Last year the cash rich retailer hit the acquisition trail in a break with its conservative past, buying U.S. credit information services company Experian. Several more deals have followed, including a property joint venture with British Land Plc and the purchase of Direct Marketing Technology Inc., a U.S. marketing information services company.
The corporate activity followed the arrival of Lord Wolfson of Sunningdale as chairman last summer, and there are hopes that he can shake up mail order and reverse the decline in its performance.
GUS has already started investing to improve the quality and service of the business. But the bulk of its home shopping remains in the declining agency market.

The firm is looking at ways to capitalise on fast growing direct mail, the sector of the market where rivals, including Burton Group Plc and Marks and Spencer Plc have moved in quickly to capitalise on shoppers' preference for small branded catalogues over the traditional agency-style big books.
"The market is looking for evidence on what GUS is doing about home shopping," said one retail analyst, who asked not to be identified.

There has been speculation GUS might share some of its cash with investors via a special dividend. It has handed cash to shareholders in the past, but some analysts were sceptical of a special payout on this occasion.
The fact that GUS brought its results forward to predate the Labour government's first budget on July 2 helped fuel the special payout talk, analysts said.
Boots Co Plc paid a special dividend with its results earlier in June, which prompted speculation this was timed to beat any tax changes in the upcoming budget.
But in fact, GUS published the date for its results back in March, well before any date for the post-election budget was even talked about, analysts said.
